paper_a.title: State-independent proof of Kochen-Specker theorem with 13 rays

metadata.description: Both papers establish the Kochen-Specker no-go theorem in the qutrit Hilbert space C^3 by exhibiting a small explicit witness ray-set, but use fundamentally different witness sets and proof strategies. Paper A (Yu-Oh 2012) constructs 13 rays {y_k^pm, h_alpha, z_k} on a magic cube and proves KS either via a direct value-assignment lemma (at most one h_alpha can be 1, vs the QM operator identity sum h_alpha = 4/3 I) or via a state-independent KS inequality (classical bound 8, quantum value 25/3). Paper B (Cabello 2025) extends to a 33-vector / 14-basis set that explicitly contains the Yu-Oh 13-ray set as a sub-configuration (DP469.2) and proves KS via a pigeonhole combinatorial argument: the embedded Yu-Oh constraint admits at most three 1-assignments while four mutually orthogonal color triples each demand one. The pair is best classified as AP (alternative proof of the same KS theorem in the same dimension), with the additional observation that paper B's construction structurally embeds paper A's set and reuses paper A's at-most-one-h_alpha lemma as a citation.

matches.explanation: Both encode the Kochen-Specker no-go statement and its underlying KS-set definition. TP410.1 is the cited Kochen-Specker theorem (no NCHV in dim>2). DP469.1 is the standard KS-set definition: a finite set of unit vectors admitting no {0,1}-assignment respecting orthogonality and basis-completeness. Both cite Kochen & Specker 1967 as origin. The two nodes are the same external mathematical object expressed once as theorem (paper A) and once as definition (paper B); the cross-type match is justified because DP469.1 packages the no-go content into the very definition of a KS set.

Paper A's notion of a KS value assignment is split across DP410.4 (definition) and AssumP410.1 (the two conditions: basis-independence of the {0,1} value, exactly one ray = 1 per orthonormal basis). Paper B's DP469.1 packs the same two conditions into the negation that defines a KS set: f(u)+f(v) <= 1 for orthogonal pairs (basis-independence + at-most-one-1) and sum_b f(u) = 1 for every basis (exactly-one-1). Same mathematical assignment rule.

Paper A's 13 magic-cube rays {y_k^pm, h_alpha, z_k} (defined in DP410.6 with explicit coordinates in EP410.1) is exactly what paper B calls the 'Yu-Oh set' (DP469.2): the 13 unit vectors in C^3 admitting KS assignments only if at most one of the four central h_alpha nodes is 1. Paper B treats it as an external object cited from Yu & Oh 2012 (i.e., paper A itself); paper A is the origin of the construction.

DP410.5 (qutrit ray representation r=(a,b,c) for |r>=a|0>+b|1>+c|2>) is the elementary notational setup for paper A's coordinate-wise ray listing. Paper B uses standard Dirac notation directly without an analogous explicit definition; this is presentational scaffolding, not a substantive concept missing from B.

Paper A's orthogonality graph Delta_13 with adjacency matrix Gamma is central to its inequality formulation (TP410.5, TP410.6, TP410.7). Paper B uses orthogonality structure throughout (color triples, Fig.~1 graph) but does not name an explicit orthogonality-graph object as a definition; the closest is the implicit graph used in TP469.2 (independence-number bound), which is a cited external result. No clean B-counterpart at the definitional level.

DP410.3 (product rule and sum rule on compatible-observable values) is paper A's algebraic axiomatization of NCHV models in the original-rule KS setting. Paper B works directly with KS {0,1}-assignments and never invokes a product/sum rule on observables; it stays purely at the value-assignment level. This is a paper-A-original framing with no B-counterpart.

DP410.1 (non-contextual hidden-variable model with HV distribution rho_lambda) is paper A's formal NCHV model. Paper B does not define an NCHV model explicitly; it operates at the level of KS value functions only. The conceptual content is implicit in paper B's KS-set definition but not surfaced as its own node.

DP410.2 (context as maximal compatible set) is paper A's definition of measurement context. Paper B speaks of contexts in the nonlocal-game and orthogonality-graph language (e.g. ProbP469.1, TP469.2) but does not isolate the maximal-compatible-set definition; closest implicit usage is via 'complete orthogonal basis' (DP469.3), but the levels differ enough to leave this unmatched.

DP410.8 (dichotomic observables A_v = I - 2 r_v with eigenvalues +/-1) is needed for paper A's state-independent KS inequality (TP410.6) and operator identity (TP410.7). Paper B's proof of KS impossibility (PP469.1) uses only {0,1} value assignments and does not introduce +/-1 dichotomic observables. Specific to paper A's inequality route.

Both make a uniqueness statement about the underlying KS construction. TP410.2 says the 13-ray Yu-Oh realization is unique up to a global unitary given the orthogonality graph Delta_13. PrP469.1 says the Cabello-33 KS set is unique up to unitaries (in contrast to Peres-33 and Penrose-33). Different sets, parallel uniqueness claims; both rely on graph-determined-by-orthogonality arguments (PrP469.1 cites the Xu et al. 2022 method).

Paper A's at-most-one-h_alpha lemma (TP410.3: at most one of h_0,...,h_3 is assigned 1 in any KS labeling of the 13 rays) is exactly the constraint paper B cites and applies in PSP469.1 ('the Yu-Oh set admits KS assignments only if at most one of its four nonwhite (central) nodes is assigned 1'). Cross-type match (theorem vs proof_step) justified because PSP469.1 functions as the invocation of paper A's TP410.3 inside paper B's proof.

Both are the papers' main no-go theorems specialized to qutrit. TP410.4 (original-rule version: classical bound sum<h_alpha>_c <= 1 vs QM 4/3) and TP410.6 (state-independent KS inequality: 8 vs 25/3) are paper A's two proofs of KS using 13 rays. TP469.1 is paper B's main theorem: the Cabello-33 set is a KS set with 14 bases. All three say 'we exhibit a finite witness in C^3 admitting no KS assignment' but with different witness sizes (13 vs 33) and different inequality vs combinatorial framings. Genuine analogue of role; not exact because the bounds and witness sets differ.

TP410.5 is the combinatorial inequality on Delta_13: sum a_v - (1/4) sum Gamma_uv a_u a_v <= 8 over +/-1 vertex labelings. This is the classical-bound side of paper A's state-independent KS inequality and has no counterpart in paper B, which proves KS combinatorially via pigeonhole on color triples rather than via a graph-theoretic +/-1-labeling bound.

TP410.7 (operator identity L = 25/3 I obtained by expanding A_v = I - 2 r_v on the magic-cube graph) is the quantum-side of paper A's state-independent inequality. Paper B has no operator-identity computation; its quantum content is the maximally entangled state (EP469.4) and the perfect-strategy claim W_Q = 1 (EP469.6). Different quantum machinery.
EP410.2 is the original-rule KS inequality sum<h_alpha>_c <= 1 (the integrated form of TP410.3). Paper B has no analogous integrated-bound equation.

EP410.3 is the operator-form magic-cube inequality (LHS sum<A_v> - (1/4) sum Gamma_uv <A_u . A_v> <= 8). Paper B does not state an operator-form KS inequality; its quantum machinery is the bipartite perfect strategy (EP469.6: W_Q = 1).

EP410.4 (operator-sum identities y = 2I, h = (4/3)I, z = I) underpins paper A's operator identity L = 25/3 I. Paper B has no analogous operator-sum bookkeeping; it works at the level of vector orthogonality and KS assignments only.

PP410.1 is paper A's proof of the 13-ray uniqueness (TP410.2). Paper B's analogous uniqueness (PrP469.1) is stated without an in-paper proof (cites Trandafir & Cabello 2026 in preparation, and Xu et al. 2022 method).

Both proofs establish KS impossibility on a small qutrit ray-set via combinatorial case analysis on the assumed 1-assignments. Paper A's PP410.2 is a two-case argument (PSP410.1: h_0,h_1 both = 1 forces z_2,z_3 both = 1, contradiction; PSP410.2: h_1,h_2 both = 1 forces z_1,z_2 both = 1, contradiction) yielding 'at most one h_alpha is 1'. Paper B's PP469.1 invokes the Yu-Oh constraint (PSP469.1, which is exactly the conclusion of paper A's PP410.2), then observes four color triples each demand one 1 (PSP469.2), then derives a pigeonhole contradiction (PSP469.3). The proofs are at different levels: paper A proves the at-most-one-h lemma directly; paper B uses it as a black box and builds a higher-level combinatorial contradiction. Both proceed by ruling out joint 1-assignments via orthogonality. Composite many-to-many entry covers the parent proofs and their step decompositions per the v2 L2-with-parent rule.

PP410.3 (proof of TP410.4: original-rule KS proof by integrating the at-most-one-h_alpha bound against rho_lambda and comparing to the QM operator identity sum h_alpha = 4/3 I) is specific to paper A's NCHV inequality framing. Paper B does not run the integration-against-rho_lambda argument.

PP410.4 and its six step nodes prove the +/-1 combinatorial bound L = 1+t+f-2l <= 8 by case analysis on t = number of -1-vertices in {0,...,6}. This is the case-by-case proof of paper A's classical KS-inequality bound (TP410.5). Paper B has no analogue: it proves KS via pigeonhole on color classes, not via a +/-1 labeling bound.

PP410.5 (proof of operator identity L = 25/3 I via expansion in r_v, edge count 24, vertex degree counts, and orthogonality r_u r_v = 0 for adjacent u,v) and its three step nodes are the operator-algebra side of paper A's state-independent inequality. Paper B's quantum content is entirely the bipartite-game perfect strategy (AP469.1) and uses no operator-identity computation.

Both papers state a problem to be solved via their KS construction. ProbP410.1 asks for an experimentally testable inequality with as few qutrit observables as possible that distinguishes NCHV from QM (state-independent contextuality test). ProbP469.1 is a bipartite nonlocal game (|X|=5, |Y|=9) seeking a perfect quantum strategy. Both are operationalizations of contextuality via small qutrit setups, but at different operational levels (single-system inequality vs bipartite game), so analogous rather than exact.

Both papers conjecture minimality of their construction. ClP410.1 conjectures that no state-independent KS proof exists with fewer than 13 rays in the qutrit. CnjP469.2 conjectures the 14-basis 33-vector set reaches the natural lower limit for the smallest qutrit KS set; CnjP469.1 conjectures the simplest qutrit KS set must contain the Yu-Oh set. Paper B's pair of conjectures together encode the analogous minimality + structural-embedding claim consistent with paper A's lower-bound conjecture; the metric (rays vs bases vs subset structure) differs.

DP469.4 (state-independent contextuality SI-C set) and TP469.3 (Yu-Oh minimality for SI-C) are external-cited results in paper B coming from Cabello, Kleinmann & Portillo 2016. These post-date paper A and are not present in it. Paper B uses them to motivate its construction; paper A predates the SI-C-vs-KS-set distinction.

Weyl-Heisenberg generators X, Z (DP469.5, EP469.7) and the proposition that acting with X and Z^2 on the Yu-Oh set produces the 33-vector KS set (PrP469.2) are paper-B-original (or Bengtsson private communication) constructions. They explain how paper B's larger set arises from paper A's 13 rays as an X, Z^2 orbit. No counterpart in paper A.

SIC-POVM (DP469.6) and the proposition that two unitarily inequivalent SIC-POVMs sit inside the 33-vector KS set (PrP469.3) are external structural observations specific to paper B's larger construction. Paper A's 13 rays do not contain a SIC-POVM (a SIC-POVM in C^3 needs 9 vectors), so this is genuinely paper-B-original content.
Majorana representation of pure spin-1 states (DP469.7) is used in paper B for visualization (ExP469.2). Paper A does not employ Majorana representation.

DP469.3 (complete orthogonal basis within a KS set) is paper B's bookkeeping definition for counting bases. Paper A enumerates orthogonality via Delta_13 instead and never makes the bases-vs-vectors distinction central; no clean A-counterpart at this definitional granularity.

DP469.8 (three vertex types of the Cabello-33 set under graph automorphisms) is structural to paper B's larger construction. Paper A has only one ray family (the 13 magic-cube rays) and no automorphism-orbit decomposition into multiple types.

Equations EP469.1-EP469.3 list Alice's and Bob's bases for the 5x9 nonlocal game, and EP469.4 is the maximally entangled qutrit-qutrit state |psi> = (1/sqrt 3) sum |j>|j>. All are bipartite-game machinery introduced by paper B; paper A is a single-system KS-inequality paper with no bipartite-game content.

Classical winning probability W_C = 44/45 (EP469.5) and quantum W_Q = 1 (EP469.6) are the bipartite-game numerical results of paper B. Paper A's analogous classical-vs-quantum gap is sum<h_alpha>_c <= 1 vs 4/3 (or LHS <= 8 vs 25/3), which is single-system; not the same operational quantity.

AP469.1 is paper B's perfect quantum strategy for the 5x9 game (share |psi>, each measure in assigned basis, output the result), with three algorithm steps (distribute bases, joint measurement, output nonorthogonal vectors). Paper A has no algorithm or quantum protocol; its quantum statement is the operator identity on a single qutrit. No parent algorithm to align against.

TP469.2 (independence-number bound W_C^max = alpha(G)/C for nonlocal-game classical winning probability) is an external cited result (Cabello, Severini, Winter 2014). It is graph-theoretic machinery for paper B's bipartite-game analysis; paper A predates and does not use this framework.

TP469.4 (KS sets are necessary for nonsignaling-limit bipartite correlations and pseudotelepathy) is an external cited result (Cabello 2025, Liu et al. 2024) that motivates paper B's interest in minimizing KS-set complexity. Paper A predates this motivation.

ClP469.1 (refutation of Cabello 2025 Conjecture 2 via the new 5x9 perfect strategy) and ClP469.2 (minimality of |X|x|Y| within the new KS set) are paper-B-specific claims about the bipartite-game operational consequences of the 33-vector construction. Not present in paper A.
